context: 3 Our use of the term “noisy super-resolution scaling” differs from that in [20], where the term refers to classical super-resolution scaling in the presence of small noise. We note that, in this definition, the error ϵ may also depend on other parameters, which we suppress in the onotation. Throughout this paper, the estimation error ϵ is measured in the matching distance (see Eq. (I.9)). 2 The 1/8 factor is an arbitrary constant that we chose. We conjecture that any constant strictly less than one (say, 0.999) could work by slightly changing the proof, but we have not checked the proof in detail with this modification. 2345 The main contribution of this paper is a significant improvement over the central limit error scaling outlined in Theorem I.2. We establish that ESPRIT achieves the optimal error scaling for estimating dominant locations and dominant intensities (Theorem I.4). To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a noisy superresolution scaling (in the sense of Definition I.1) for spectral estimation under comparable assumptions. a) Notation.: A complete summary of our notation is provided in Appendix A-A. We make special comments about our use of asymptotic notation. Throughout this paper, most of our results are non-asymptotic, and we use the big-O notation f (n) = O (g(n)) to indicate that there exists a universal constant C > 0 such that f (n) ≤ C · g(n). Similarly, f (n) = Ω(g(n)) or f (n) = Θ(g(n)) imply the existence of a uniform constant C > 0 such that f (n) ≥ C · g(n) or C −1 · g(n) ≤ f (n) ≤ C · g(n). We augment O (B), Ω(B), and Θ(B) with a tilde to suppress polylogarithmic factors in B.
